query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Surface modification of refractory high-entropy alloys through coating or alloying with oxygen-resistant elements will improve their high-temperature oxygen resistance by forming a protective surface layer.
generation.intervention: Surface modification through coating or alloying with oxygen-resistant elements
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a protective surface layer
generation.mechanism: Improved thermal oxidation resistance due to the formation of a protective surface layer
generation.uncertainty: The exact extent of improvement in high-temperature oxygen resistance may vary depending on the specific surface modification technique and oxygen-resistant elements used.

falsification_experiment.design: Compare the high-temperature oxygen resistance of surface-modified RHEAs with that of untreated RHEAs under identical conditions.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the surface-modified RHEAs do not exhibit significantly improved high-temperature oxygen resistance compared to the untreated RHEAs, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-temperature oxidation-resistant VZrHfNbTa refractory HEA-based Hf-coated composites are prepared by the combined process. It has a coating thickness of 120 μm. Vanadium, niobium, tantalum and hafnium elements in the base alloy have obvious boundaries with the hafnium coating, and the zirconium element undergoes diffusion and migration in the coating with a diffusive distance of about 60 μm. High-temperature oxidation tests show that the weight gain per unit area of the coated sample is much less than that of the uncoated sample. Dents and pulverization on the surface of the alloy after oxidation of the uncoated specimen, oxidation, and sintering on the surface of the coated specimen result in the formation of a dense HfO2 protective layer. The coating can effectively improve the oxidation resistance of the material in extreme environments and prevent the surface from chalking, thus extending the material’s service life and broadening the application. AbstractIn this paper, the Si-20Cr-20Fe coating was prepared on MoNbTaTiW RHEA by a fused slurry method. The microstructural evolution and compositions of the silicide coating under high-temperature oxidation environment were studied. The results show that the silicide coating could effectively prevent the oxidation of the MoNbTaTiW RHEA. The initial silicide coating had a double-layer structure: a high silicon content layer mainly composed of MSi2 as the outer layer and a low silicon content layer mainly contained M5Si3 as the inner layer. Under high-temperature oxidation conditions, the silicon element diffused from the silicide coating to the RHEA substrate while the oxidation of the coating occurred. After oxidation, the coating was composed of an outer oxide layer and an inner silicide layer. The silicide layer moved toward the inside of the substrate, led to the increase of its thickness. Compared with the initial silicified layer, its structure did not change significantly. The structure and compositions of the oxide layer on the outer surface strongly depended on the oxidation temperature.
